posts.author: StudioYebisu
posts.text:
たった今、世界のAI覇権のバランスは完全にぶっ壊れました。これほんまにやばいです。
週明けのAI関連株は大暴落どころの騒ぎじゃないかもな…。
何が衝撃的なのか、ガチ解説します。
もう何もかもが変わっちまったんだな...。

■何がおきたか
DeepSeek v4.1-Flash 1017というモデルが公開されました。世界のAI情勢を破壊します。ヤバいモデルです。
このモデル簡単がどういうものなのか説明すると、
フロンティアモデルを一部で越える（SOTA級）のモデルを中華ラボがいきなり出してきた。

問題はその性能、値段とサイズと仕組み
どれも本当に破壊的なものだから、1個ずついきます。

■性能
全分野でOpus5.5を超えたっていうわけじゃないけど。
完全にDeepSeek v4.1-Flash 1017はSOTA級

DeepSWEっていうベンチが一番衝撃的かな。
- 今回のFlash：成功率77%、約0.20ドル／タスク
- GPT-6.1 Solの最も高得点の設定：約75%、約0.65ドル／タスク
つまり、この比較では約3分の1の費用で、成功率も少し高い。大量に実装・修正を回す用途には大きな差。
というか、成功率でSolを越えてるっていう事実がヤバいんだよ。

■値段
もう完全に乱暴に言うと。ほぼタダです。<言い過ぎ
INPUT$0.15Output$0.3

入力10万＋出力1万トークンの例だと
Solより約86〜93%安く、Opusより約93〜97%安い
DeepSeekハーネスを使えば、自分の利用では、入力のキャッシュヒット率が99%になることもあったので。
実際はもっと安い。
過去に湯水のように使えるAstra,Opus,Fableをくれとは言ったが。ここまでやれとは言ってない。
本当に、なんだろう、マジで安いんだよ。
実際の感覚だと200倍ぐらい安いね。

■サイズ
これだけヤバいモデルのオープンウェイトが同時に無料公開されました。
そのサイズは763B。重みだけで約510.3GB

例えば米国のフロンティアモデルのサイズは10Tとか言われてるんですね、公開情報じゃないからわからん無いけど。Kimi K3とかが2.8T

要するに、めちゃくちゃサイズが小さいんですよ。
このパラメータ数って多ければ多いほど計算に計算資源と電力がかかるんで、コストかかるんですよ。

アメリカのAIモデルって、バカみたいに計算資源を保有してるからゴリ押しでそれを解決してるんですけど。

こんだけ軽かったら、もう普通に家で使えるレベルなんですよ。

実際、DGXSpark × 4台とかMacStudio 512GBで動かせると思います。
バカみたいなデータセンターがなくても、フロンティアモデルが動くようになっちゃったってわけ。

■仕組み
ここがかなり驚き度の高いポイントなんですけど。
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash自体はもともと存在していて。
まあそこそこ人気だったんですけど。本当に安くてそこそこ性能いいから、結構人気あるよね、ぐらいの賢さだったんですよ。

そのもともとあったモデルを自己フィードバックを使うRLで強化した。って公式は言ってて。
まあ詳しい説明は省きますけど。要するに、既に存在していたモデルを後から調整していくようなやり方で、とんでもなく性能をあげた。

驚くのは、既存モデルの後学習で、開発タスクの成功率を上げながら、処理時間や出力量まで減らしたところです。性能を上げたうえで、使う側の費用まで下げてきた。その性能の上り方が半端じゃないんだよ…意味わかんねぇよ…

DeepSeekのラボが今世界で最もAI、優れたAIラボであるということを認めなきゃいけない。

THIS IS A PURE F*CKING GOLDMINE

Anthropic just shared the sharpest trick for Claude Code

The idea: let Opus 5.5 write the plan as a script, and swarm the new Haiku 5.5 in parallel

Huge sweeps with zero Opus burn: the script holds the loop and Opus only sees the final diff

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model opus --effort ultracode

here's the split:

→ Opus 5.5 turns your objective into an executable workflow script
→ Haiku 5.5 swarms every file in parallel at 340 tok/s to extract candidates
→ Sonnet 5.5 patches each fix and cross-checks findings in its own isolated copy
→ you stop burning Opus context on a hundred agent transcripts

Opus only shows up at three moments:

→ authoring the workflow script before the run
→ reading verified findings after the swarm finishes
→ signing off before anything ships to git

Opus plans · Haiku scans · Sonnet ships

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

> Opus 5.5 runs the main session and writes workflow.js
> pipeline() fans out the new Haiku 5.5 to audit every file
> parallel() schema validators drop false positives in V8
> Sonnet 5.5 patches each fix in an isolated worktree

> Opus 5.5 reads only what survived verification
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

posts.author: Arindam Majumder 𝕏
posts.text:
people keep confusing Jev with tabular foundation models.

they're not the same thing.

the difference comes down to one thing:

Jev does zero-shot classification. TFMs make predictions grounded in learned data.

here's the breakdown.

Jev: unstructured in → structured out

Jev takes text or other inputs and turns them into decisions.

→ is this lead worth pursuing? 
→ should this email get a reply? 
→ which agent should handle this task? 
→ does this document need further review?

it's built for lightweight, low-cost classification and decision routing, without needing task-specific training data.

Tabular foundation models: structured data in → grounded predictions out

Models like TabPFN learn patterns from tabular data to classify outcomes or predict numerical values.

they use learned patterns in data to make predictions grounded in the examples they see.

this isn't zero-shot classification in the same sense as Jev.

but here's where it gets interesting.

imagine combining both to build predictive agents.

Jev handles the fast decisions: classify incoming information, route tasks, and decide what needs attention.

a tabular foundation model handles the predictions: estimate risks, forecast outcomes, and score opportunities using structured data.

one decides what to do next. the other predicts what might happen.

that's a much more interesting architecture than asking one massive LLM to do everything.

the future of AI agents might not be about finding one model that does it all.

it might be about getting different models to work together.

THIS IS A PURE F*CKING GOLDMINE

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: let Opus 5.5 write the plan as a script, and let 12 cheap agents run it while Opus sits idle at zero tokens.

Same task, two ways: Opus solo was 49% done and still running. The swarm finished in 9 minutes on 165k tokens.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model opus --swarm haiku,sonnet

here's the split:

→ Opus 5.5 writes plan.js, then stops reading anything
→ 6 Haiku 5.5 agents audit every file in parallel
→ 4 Sonnet 5.5 agents patch each fix in its own isolated copy
→ 2 Haiku 5.5 agents cross-check, 8 of 9 findings survive
Opus only shows up at two moments:
→ writing the plan before the run
→ signing off on the verified fixes after it
Opus plans. Haiku scans. Sonnet ships.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: 3,767 forks this run - which model, which lane, retry or stop - resolved in code, and only the genuinely split ones ever reach Opus

the full tree
> Opus 5.5 runs the main session on xhigh and writes plan.js
> scan audits each file on Haiku 5.5, six in parallel
> patch applies each fix on Sonnet 5.5 in its own isolated copy
> verify cross-checks every finding on Haiku 5.5
> Opus 5.5 reads only what survived, then signs off
> JEV resolves micro-forks in milliseconds

paste the tree and this prompt into Claude Code ↓

"Rebuild my Claude Code setup around this tree:

Run the main session on Opus 5.5 with effort xhigh and swarm haiku,sonnet.
Have Opus write the plan as a script: scan on Haiku 5.5, patch on Sonnet 5.5 in isolated copies, verify on Haiku 5.5.
Let the phases overlap - each finding moves on as soon as its own stage finishes, no waiting for the batch.
Never surface raw agent output to the main session, only verified results.
Route deterministic forks (model choice, lane choice, retries) through JEV.
Show me every change as a diff first. No edits until I say go."

This guy used Grok Bot to build a Quant ROC system and it made $2,847 a day on Polymarket

The result is already +$418,551 PnL in 147 days with about $261 per average trade, repeating the same setup 27 times every hour across BTC "Up or Down" markets

Several AI agents work together as one algorithm:

1. ROC measures how fast BTC is moving and in which direction

The bot compares the current BTC level with where it was a few moments earlier:

ROC = (Sₜ - Sₜ₋ₙ) / Sₜ₋ₙ × 100

Where:

Sₜ = current BTC level
Sₜ₋ₙ = BTC level at the start of the window

Strong positive ROC → stronger Up signal
Strong negative ROC → stronger Down signal

The larger the absolute ROC, the stronger the short-term move

2. ATR checks whether that move is actually large for current volatility

The system then measures the normal trading range:

TR = max(H - L, |H - Cprev|, |L - Cprev|)
ATR = Average(TR)

A signal matters only when the BTC move is large enough relative to ATR:

|Move| > k × ATR

This stops the bot from treating ordinary noise as momentum when volatility is already high

昨天还在说 Code Review 的实践，今天Anthropic就写了一篇文章详细描述它们 Code Review 的工程实践：
https://t.co/ApdUTxp8pv

非常受用，可以好好读一下，核心观点是：代码多到人读不过来之后，人已经不 review 代码了，而是追求花最少的时间 并且回滚和事故又不增加

一个改动要过七层检查，几点也很有趣：

1 让 Agent 提 PR 之前先自证 证明做完了 测试 截图 等等

2 每个 PR 都有 AI review  diff，对照整个仓库和 PR 的意图来审 多个 agent 同时找 bug 再由另一组投票，多数认定是真问题才发出来 纯风格类的意见直接丢掉 这个和我的 review-forge 的思路非常类似

3 按风险决定要几个人批 低风险不用人批准自动合并，普通功能一人批 最高风险的路径要两个人（我怀疑这步骤真的那么有用吗？人能看过来吗）

4 merge queue / feature flag / 灰度发布 先给内部员工用， 快速发现 快速回 feature flag 不用部署就能关掉

里面还有一个非常实用的思路 正好解答昨天多 agent review 的问题：

review 要能收敛，agent 写 agent 审，有可能可以互相折腾个没完，文中说有个 PR 一夜之间来回改了五十多轮 git blame 一看，59% 被反复标记的都是第一轮时就已经存在的老代码

所以他们加了几条规则：最多三轮，超过就让作者退一步重新想方案 几轮之后只审新增的 diff 已经提过的意见不再重复。

In 2022, Berkeley PhD student Woosuk Kwon thought he could make Meta's new open-weight model, OPT-175B, run faster in two weeks.

Four years and 3,000 contributors later, that project is @vllm_project, one of the largest open-source inference engines, running on ~500,000 GPUs at any given time.

He and fellow researchers Simon Mo, Kaichao You, and Roger Wang borrowed "virtual memory" from operating systems, handing out memory only as it's needed so each GPU can juggle requests of wildly different sizes. (The "v" in vLLM is for virtual.)

Their first user, Berkeley neighbor @arena, cut its GPU needs in half. Today Google, Amazon, and Meta all run vLLM in production.

In January, the core maintainers founded @inferact and raised $150M to give vLLM a full-time team.

posts.author: Arindam Majumder 𝕏
posts.text:
people keep confusing Jev with tabular foundation models.

they're not the same thing.

the difference comes down to one thing:

Jev does zero-shot classification. TFMs make predictions grounded in learned data.

here's the breakdown.

Jev: unstructured in → structured out

Jev takes text or other inputs and turns them into decisions.

→ is this lead worth pursuing? 
→ should this email get a reply? 
→ which agent should handle this task? 
→ does this document need further review?

it's built for lightweight, low-cost classification and decision routing, without needing task-specific training data.

Tabular foundation models: structured data in → grounded predictions out

Models like TabPFN learn patterns from tabular data to classify outcomes or predict numerical values.

they use learned patterns in data to make predictions grounded in the examples they see.

this isn't zero-shot classification in the same sense as Jev.

but here's where it gets interesting.

imagine combining both to build predictive agents.

Jev handles the fast decisions: classify incoming information, route tasks, and decide what needs attention.

a tabular foundation model handles the predictions: estimate risks, forecast outcomes, and score opportunities using structured data.

one decides what to do next. the other predicts what might happen.

that's a much more interesting architecture than asking one massive LLM to do everything.

posts.text:
We just open-sourced another pair of state-of-the-art Decision Models: 

pplx-decider-flash-v1.2:  4B params, 1 cent per million tokens (top 4B model on HF Decision Index)

pplx-decider-v1.2: 27B params, 2 cents per million tokens (#2 on HF Decision Index overall - for now, will improve rapidly)

Both are available on the Perplexity Decisions API as well as in the form of open weights on @huggingface 

Enjoy!
